title: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
summary: Build an application security programme: secure SDLC models, testable requirements, code review, SAST rules you write and run, secrets hooks, disclosure, and CVE triage with KEV, EPSS, SSVC and patch SLAs.
outcomes: Explain what an AppSec programme is, who owns each activity, and how SDL, SAMM, SSDF and ASVS fit together
Review a pull request for injection, IDOR and XSS, and explain why each fix works
Explain taint analysis and write a Semgrep rule and a CodeQL query, then triage false positives
Set up secrets scanning with a pre-commit hook and push protection, and respond to a leaked key
Run a vulnerability pipeline: inventory, deduplication, KEV, EPSS and CVSS ranking, and SSVC decisions
Set patch SLAs with exceptions, and choose metrics such as open age and coverage that resist gaming
Argue for programme decisions that remove bug classes: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design

lessons.title: What an application security programme is, and who owns what

blocks.md:
Picture a company with 60 engineers who ship to production several times a day, and two security engineers. The two cannot read every change, sit in every design meeting and patch every server. If security depends on them personally, it fails in the first busy week.

An **application security programme** is the answer. AppSec (application security) means the security of the software a company writes and runs, as opposed to its office network or laptops. A programme is a set of repeatable activities, named owners, tools and measurements that makes secure software the normal output of building software. Earlier courses taught single bug classes: injection, XSS, broken access control, supply chain attacks. This course is about the machine that finds and fixes them at scale.

The **SDLC** (software development life cycle) is the series of stages every piece of software passes through: requirements, design, implementation (writing code), verification (testing), release, then operation and maintenance until it is retired. A **secure SDLC** attaches a security activity to each stage.

A common slogan is **shift left**. Draw the stages on a timeline from left to right; moving a check to the left means doing it earlier, where a fix costs a changed sentence in a design document or a one-line edit, instead of an emergency patch on a live system. Shift left does not mean dropping the checks on the right: some problems only appear in running systems.

blocks.title: A secure SDLC: one security activity per stage

scenes.caption: Six stages, left to right, each with a security activity a later lesson explains: ASVS (a requirements catalogue), SAST and DAST (static and dynamic security testing), SCA and SBOM (recalled from the supply chain course).
Left side: requirements and design. A missing authorization rule caught here costs a sentence in a document. Lessons 3 and 4.
Middle: code review, static analysis and secrets checks on every change, then dependency scanning at build time. Lessons 5 to 11.
Right side: testing the running app, then operating it: finding vulnerabilities in what is deployed, taking reports from outsiders, patching on deadlines. Lessons 10 and 12 to 18.
The loop that makes it a programme: every finding and incident feeds back into requirements, rules and training, so the same bug class gets rarer.

blocks.md:
Who owns what, in a typical software company:

- **Developers** own the security of their code: they fix findings in the services they run.
- **Engineering managers and product owners** own priorities: they schedule fixes and, within policy, can accept a risk for a limited time.
- The **AppSec team** owns standards, tools, reviews of high-risk changes and help with triage. It advises and measures; it rarely writes the fix.
- **Security champions** are developers inside each team with extra security training (lesson 12).
- **Platform and IT teams** patch shared infrastructure: operating systems, databases, appliances.
- The **CISO** (chief information security officer, the executive accountable for security) owns the programme and reports risk to leadership.

Equifax shows what happens when ownership exists only on paper. You met the breach in *Security basics*: in 2017 attackers entered through an unpatched Apache Struts bug. The US House Oversight Committee report adds the programme view. Equifax's 2016 Patch Management Policy said critical vulnerabilities must be patched within 48 hours. It defined a Business Owner, a System Owner and an Application Owner for each IT asset, and made System and Application Owners keep a software inventory with version numbers.

But witnesses told the Committee there were no official designees for these roles. Asked who the application owner of the breached dispute portal was, one official said they did not believe there was any explicit designation. The patch alert went out as an email to a mailing list. A rule with no named owner is a wish.

blocks.code:
# .github/CODEOWNERS: GitHub requests a review from these owners
# whenever a pull request changes a matching path.
*                        @acme/platform
/services/payments/      @acme/payments-team
/services/*/auth/        @acme/payments-team @acme/appsec
/infra/terraform/iam/    @acme/appsec
/.github/workflows/      @acme/appsec
blocks.caption: A CODEOWNERS file (GitHub's format; team names made up) turns ownership into something the tooling enforces. With branch protection set to require code owner review, changes to login code, cloud permissions or CI pipelines cannot merge without the AppSec team. The last matching line wins.

blocks.md: A programme is owners plus deadlines plus measurement. For every activity in this course, ask three questions: which named person or team does it, by when, and which number shows that it actually happens?

"Security owns security" is the most common misconception. A central team that tries to fix everything becomes a bottleneck and then gets bypassed. The working model: developers own fixes, the security team owns the system that makes fixes happen.

blocks.question: Equifax's 2016 policy required critical patches within 48 hours and defined business, system and application owners. Why did that not get Struts patched on the dispute portal, according to the House report?
options: The roles existed in the policy, but nobody was officially designated to fill them, so the emailed alert reached no accountable owner
The 48-hour deadline was too short to be realistic
Apache had not yet released a fix
The policy only covered Windows servers
blocks.explain: The report says roles were defined but there were no official designees, and an official could not name the portal's application owner. A deadline only works when a named owner receives it and is measured on it.

blocks.question: A team moves its dependency check from a quarterly audit to every pull request. What does "shift left" mean here?
options: The check now happens earlier in the life cycle, when a fix is cheaper
The check is now run by the left-most team on the org chart
The quarterly audit is no longer needed for anything
Findings are now sorted from lowest to highest severity
blocks.explain: On a left-to-right timeline of the SDLC, earlier is left. Finding a vulnerable dependency in the pull request that adds it costs one line; finding it in production costs an incident. Later checks still catch what early ones miss.

lessons.title: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF

blocks.md: You do not have to invent a programme from nothing. Three public documents describe one, each from a different angle. Tiny example of why you need more than one: a startup asks "what should we do?" (a list of practices), "how good are we now?" (a maturity score) and "what will our government customer ask us to attest to?" (a standard). Three questions, three documents.

**Microsoft SDL** (Security Development Lifecycle). Microsoft says it launched its Trustworthy Computing initiative in January 2002, as malicious software spread to home PCs newly connected to the internet, and that the SDL became an integral part of its development process in 2004. Microsoft's own description has seven components: five core phases (requirements, design, implementation, verification, release) and two supporting activities (training before, response after).

Verification is the concrete part. A manual review by someone who is not the code's author (separation of duties), plus automated checks in the pipeline: static code analysis, binary analysis, a credential and secret scanner, encryption scanning, fuzz testing (feeding a program huge numbers of malformed inputs to find crashes), configuration validation, and component governance (open-source detection with version and vulnerability checks). Releases then go out in rings: the team, then all employees, then early customers, then everyone.

**OWASP SAMM** (Software Assurance Maturity Model). OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project you met in earlier courses, publishes it; SAMM's site says Pravir Chandra wrote the original model in 2009. A maturity model measures how established a practice is in your organisation. SAMM version 2 has **5 business functions** (Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations), each with **3 security practices**, 15 in total. Each practice has activities in two streams and **3 maturity levels**. SAMM says plainly that it does not expect everyone to reach the top level everywhere: you pick a target per practice.

The 15 practices, function by function: Governance (Strategy and Metrics, Policy and Compliance, Education and Guidance); Design (Threat Assessment, Security Requirements, Secure Architecture); Implementation (Secure Build, Secure Deployment, Defect Management); Verification (Architecture Assessment, Requirements-driven Testing, Security Testing); Operations (Incident Management, Environment Management, Operational Management).

blocks.title: A SAMM self-assessment: current, target, gap (example scores)

scenes.caption: Current scores for an imagined mid-size company, 0 (nothing) to 3 (highest maturity), one row per business function, one column per practice in the order listed above. Made-up numbers for illustration.
The target the company sets for next year. Not all 3s: SAMM asks you to choose targets by risk. A payments company might push Defect Management harder than a game studio.
Gap = target minus current. The roadmap is the cells with the largest gaps: here Threat Assessment, Security Requirements and Defect Management, two levels each.

blocks.md:
**NIST SSDF** (Secure Software Development Framework), published by NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) as Special Publication 800-218, version 1.1 (2022). It does not invent new practices; it collects them from existing guides (BSA, The Software Alliance, a software industry group; OWASP; SAFECode, the Software Assurance Forum for Excellence in Code; and others) and maps each task to them. Practices fall into four groups:

- **PO**, Prepare the Organization: people, processes and tools ready for secure development.
- **PS**, Protect the Software: all components protected from tampering and unauthorised access.
- **PW**, Produce Well-Secured Software: minimal vulnerabilities in releases.
- **RV**, Respond to Vulnerabilities: find residual vulnerabilities, fix them, and prevent similar ones.

The SSDF matters commercially: CISA's Secure Software Development Attestation Form, which software producers selling to the US federal government sign, is based on SSDF practices.

blocks.code:
# controls.yaml: our pipeline, mapped to SSDF v1.1 task IDs
- control: Code stored in GitHub, protected branches, 2FA enforced
  ssdf: PS.1.1        # store all forms of code, restrict access
- control: Policy says which changes need human security review
  ssdf: PW.7.1        # decide whether code review or analysis is used
- control: Peer review plus Semgrep and CodeQL on every pull request
  ssdf: PW.7.2        # perform the code review and/or code analysis
- control: DAST baseline scan and fuzzing in CI
  ssdf: PW.8.2        # scope, design and perform executable testing
- control: Watch NVD, KEV and vendor advisories daily
  ssdf: RV.1.1        # gather information on potential vulnerabilities
- control: security.txt plus a published disclosure policy
  ssdf: RV.1.3        # policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation
- control: Every finding gets a ticket with a risk score
  ssdf: RV.2.1        # analyse each vulnerability to plan remediation
blocks.caption: A mapping file like this is how teams answer an SSDF attestation questionnaire: each claim points at a real control that someone can inspect. The task IDs are from SP 800-218.

blocks.md: SDL says what one company does, SAMM measures how mature you are, and SSDF is the reference list that governments and customers ask you to attest to. Most programmes use SAMM to plan and SSDF to report.

blocks.question: A CISO wants to show the board that the company improved its threat modelling over a year, with a number. Which framework is built for that?
options: NIST SSDF, because it lists practices with task IDs
Microsoft SDL, because it has seven components
OWASP SAMM, because it scores each practice on maturity levels and supports a target per practice
None: security cannot be measured
blocks.explain: SAMM is a maturity model: it scores practices such as Threat Assessment from 0 to 3, so you can report current, target and progress. SSDF lists what to do, and SDL describes Microsoft's process; neither scores maturity.

blocks.question: In SSDF terms, running a vulnerability disclosure programme falls under which group?
options: PO, Prepare the Organization
PS, Protect the Software
PW, Produce Well-Secured Software
RV, Respond to Vulnerabilities
blocks.explain: Task RV.1.3 is having a policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation. RV covers everything after release: finding residual vulnerabilities, fixing them and preventing repeats.

lessons.title: Security requirements you can test: OWASP ASVS levels

blocks.md:
"The app must be secure" is not a requirement: nobody can test it. "A logged-in user can only read invoices they own, and asking for someone else's returns 404" is a requirement: a test can pass or fail. A **security requirement** is a testable statement about how the software must behave so that a class of attack fails.

Writing these from scratch for every project is slow and uneven, so most teams start from a catalogue. The best known for web applications is the **OWASP ASVS** (Application Security Verification Standard). OWASP describes it as a basis for testing web application security controls and a list of requirements for secure development. Version 5.0.0 was published on 30 May 2025.

ASVS 5.0.0 has 17 chapters, from V1 Encoding and Sanitization to V17 WebRTC. Every requirement has an ID of the form chapter.section.requirement. Because IDs move between versions, OWASP asks you to quote the version too: `v5.0.0-1.2.4` means requirement 4 in section 2 (Injection Prevention) of chapter 1, as of 5.0.0.

Each requirement also has a **level**, L1 to L3:

- **L1**: the minimum, critical first-layer defences against common attacks that need no other vulnerability to work. About 20% of the requirements.
- **L2**: what OWASP says most applications should aim for: less common attacks, or stronger protections against common ones. Complying with L2 means meeting all L1 and L2 requirements.
- **L3**: the remaining requirements, for applications that must show the highest assurance. OWASP's own example: an early-stage startup holding little sensitive data might target L1, while a bank would struggle to justify less than L3 for online banking.

blocks.title: ASVS 5.0.0 requirements by level (counted from OWASP's CSV)

scenes.caption: Counted from the official 5.0.0 requirements CSV: 70 requirements are tagged L1, 183 L2 and 92 L3, 345 in total.
What you must meet to claim each level, because levels are cumulative: 70 for L1, 253 for L2, all 345 for L3. L1 is about 20% of the standard, L2 about 73%.

blocks.md:
Three L1 requirements, quoted from 5.0.0, that match the bug classes from your prerequisite courses:

- **v5.0.0-1.2.4**: data selection or database queries use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL injection and other database injection.
- **v5.0.0-8.2.2**: data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items, to mitigate IDOR and BOLA.
- **v5.0.0-1.2.1**: output encoding for an HTTP response, HTML document or XML document fits the context (HTML elements, attributes, comments, CSS, header fields).

And two that link straight to patching later in this course: **15.1.1** (L1) asks that documentation defines risk-based remediation time frames for vulnerable third-party components, and **15.2.1** (L1) asks that the application contains only components that have not breached those time frames.

blocks.code:
# test_authz.py: ASVS v5.0.0-8.2.2 written as an automated test (pytest)
def test_user_cannot_read_another_users_invoice(client, make_invoice):
    theirs = make_invoice(owner_id=2, title="Bob salary")

    r = client.get(f"/invoices/{theirs}", headers={"X-Test-User": "1"})

    assert r.status_code == 404   # our design: don't confirm it exists


def test_user_can_read_own_invoice(client, make_invoice):
    mine = make_invoice(owner_id=1, title="Alice rent")
    r = client.get(f"/invoices/{mine}", headers={"X-Test-User": "1"})
    assert r.status_code == 200
blocks.caption: A requirement becomes a regression test that runs on every change. The `client` and `make_invoice` fixtures are the app's own test helpers. The header stands in for login in this test app. Lesson 6 reviews the code this test protects.

blocks.md: Do not adopt all 345 requirements in week one. Pick a target level per application by risk, copy the relevant chapters into your own requirements list, drop what does not apply (no GraphQL, no WebRTC), and link each requirement to a test or a review checklist item.

blocks.question: Your team says its app is "ASVS Level 2 compliant" but has only checked the L2-tagged requirements. What is missing?
options: Nothing, L2 compliance means meeting the L2-tagged requirements
The L3 requirements, which are always included
All the L1 requirements: levels are cumulative, so L2 means every L1 and L2 requirement
A CVSS score for each requirement
blocks.explain: OWASP says complying with L2 means implementing about 70% of the standard: all L1 and L2 requirements. Skipping L1 would skip the most basic first-layer defences.

blocks.question: Which statement is a testable security requirement?
options: The API should be protected against hackers
Use best practices for authentication
Every endpoint returning an invoice checks that the invoice's owner_id equals the logged-in user's id, otherwise it returns 404
Security is everyone's responsibility
blocks.explain: Only this one says exactly what behaviour must happen, so a test can pass or fail. The others are wishes or slogans; they cannot be verified.

lessons.title: Design review in the cycle: deciding which changes get a threat model

blocks.md:
Recall from *Threat modelling principles*: a threat model answers four questions (what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, did we do a good job), usually with a data flow diagram and STRIDE. That course showed how to do one. The programme question is different: a company merges hundreds of changes a week, and an AppSec team can hold perhaps a handful of design reviews. Which changes get one?

Tiny example. Change A renames a button. Change B adds a public API endpoint. Change C adds a new payment provider that will store card data and call a third-party service. A sensible programme spends zero security minutes on A, a short checklist on B, and a full design review with a threat model on C.

The tool for this is **risk-based triage**: a short questionnaire in the design document template whose answers decide the review depth. The triggers are the things your threat models keep finding dangerous:

- a new entry point reachable from the internet (new attack surface)
- changes to authentication or authorization
- storing a new class of sensitive data (payment cards, health data, credentials)
- a new third party that receives data or runs code
- anything that implements its own cryptography

Microsoft's SDL makes the end of this path a gate: before a product is released, its threat models are reviewed for accuracy and completeness, including mitigations for unacceptable risks. In SAMM terms this is the Threat Assessment practice.

blocks.code:
SENSITIVE = {"payment_card", "health", "credentials"}

def design_review_level(change):
    hits = [name for name, hit in [
        ("new internet endpoint", change.get("new_endpoint")),
        ("touches auth",          change.get("touches_auth")),
        ("new sensitive data",    SENSITIVE & set(change.get("stores", []))),
        ("new third party",       change.get("new_vendor")),
        ("own cryptography",      change.get("own_crypto")),
    ] if hit]
    if "own cryptography" in hits or len(hits) >= 2:
        return "AppSec design review", hits
    if hits:
        return "champion review", hits
    return "self-serve checklist", hits

print(design_review_level({"stores": ["display_name"]}))
print(design_review_level({"new_endpoint": True}))
print(design_review_level({"new_endpoint": True, "new_vendor": True,
                           "stores": ["payment_card"]}))

# output
('self-serve checklist', [])
('champion review', ['new internet endpoint'])
('AppSec design review', ['new internet endpoint', 'new sensitive data', 'new third party'])
blocks.caption: A triage rule as code, run on the three example changes. The thresholds are a policy choice, not a standard: tune them so the AppSec team's review queue stays small enough to answer within days.

blocks.title: Three changes through design triage

scenes.caption: Every design document answers the questionnaire. The answers, not the author's opinion, pick the path.
Change A (a renamed button) hits no trigger: the team ticks a self-serve checklist and moves on. Zero AppSec time spent.
Change B (a new public endpoint) hits one trigger: the team's security champion reviews it against the checklist and ASVS items for APIs.
Change C (a payment provider) hits three: a full threat model with the AppSec team, before code is written.
Every path ends in the same place: security requirements and tickets that code review and tests later check. A review that produces no tracked requirement leaves no trace.

blocks.md: A design review that happens after the code is written is an audit, not a design review. If the triage questionnaire lives in the pull request template instead of the design template, the expensive decisions (which vendor, where the data lives) are already made.

blocks.question: Under the rule above, a change adds a new internal batch job that implements its own encryption of backup files. What review does it get, and why?
options: Self-serve checklist, because it is internal
Champion review, because it has one trigger
AppSec design review, because own cryptography is an automatic escalation regardless of the number of triggers
No review: backups are not part of the application
blocks.explain: The rule escalates any home-made cryptography straight to AppSec. Hand-built crypto fails in subtle ways that a checklist cannot catch, which is why this trigger alone is enough.

blocks.question: Why put the triage questions in the design template rather than only in pull requests?
options: Pull requests cannot contain text
Threat models are only legal at design time
Security champions cannot read pull requests
Design decisions such as data storage and vendors are cheapest to change before code exists
blocks.explain: This is shift left applied to design: the review must happen while the architecture can still change cheaply.

lessons.title: Secure code review: what a reviewer looks for

blocks.md:
Most teams already review every change before it merges. A **secure code review** is that review done with an attacker's questions in mind. OWASP's Secure Code Review Cheat Sheet defines it as manually examining source code to find security vulnerabilities that automated tools often miss, focusing on business logic, complex security implementations and context-specific flaws, and complementing SAST and DAST rather than replacing them.

The cheat sheet names two kinds. A **baseline review** reads a whole codebase: for a new application, a major release, a legacy system you just inherited, or after an incident. A **diff-based review** reads only the change in a pull request, as part of daily work. A programme runs diff-based reviews continuously and baseline reviews on a risk-based schedule.

The core technique is **data flow tracing**, the manual version of what lesson 7 automates:

1. Find the **sources**: where outside data enters (request parameters, headers, uploaded files, messages, database rows written by other users).
2. Follow the **processing**: validation, transformation, business logic.
3. Check the **sinks**: places where data becomes dangerous (SQL queries, shell commands, HTML output, file paths, redirects, deserialisers).
4. At every **trust boundary** crossing, ask whether the right check happens: input validation, output encoding, authorization.

Then the questions tools cannot answer: is this endpoint supposed to be public? Who is allowed to see this object? What happens if these two requests race?

blocks.title: Tracing one value through a change, the way a reviewer does

scenes.caption: Start where data enters. Here a query parameter arrives in the request handler. Everything from the client is attacker-controlled.
Follow it inward. Does anything validate it? Is the user allowed to touch the object the value names? Authorization belongs here, at the trust boundary.
Find every sink it reaches. A database query needs parameters, never string building.
Data coming back out is a source again for the next sink: rows written by other users must be encoded before they reach HTML.
The reviewer's notes are per arrow, not per file: each crossing either has its control or is a finding.

blocks.code:
## Security review checklist (pull request template)
- [ ] New or changed entry points listed (routes, queues, CLI flags, webhooks)
- [ ] Every new endpoint: authentication required? who may call it?
- [ ] Every object fetched by id: ownership or permission checked server-side
- [ ] Queries use parameters or the ORM; no string-built SQL, shell or paths
- [ ] Output to HTML/JS goes through the template engine's escaping
- [ ] No secrets, tokens or keys in code, config or tests
- [ ] Errors do not leak stack traces or internal data to clients
- [ ] Security-relevant events logged (login, permission denied, admin actions)
- [ ] New dependency? Why, who maintains it, what does it pull in?
- [ ] Tests added for the abuse case, not only the happy path
blocks.caption: A checklist drawn from the OWASP cheat sheet's vulnerability patterns. Its job is to make the reviewer ask the questions, not to replace thinking. Keep it short enough that people actually read it.

blocks.md: Human review finds what tools cannot. **Heartbleed** (CVE-2014-0160; named for the TLS heartbeat extension it sits in and the memory it leaks, or bleeds), the 2014 OpenSSL bug in which the server trusted a length field in a heartbeat message and sent back up to 64 KB of its own memory per request, was found independently by Codenomicon, a Finnish security testing company, and by Neel Mehta of Google Security. David A. Wheeler, a software security researcher, wrote a detailed analysis of how the bug could have been prevented. Wheeler reports, citing others, that Mehta's team found it during a source code review, and that several widely used static analysis tools (Coverity, Klocwork in its normal configuration, and GrammaTech's CodeSonar) would not have found it ahead of time. Meanwhile the bug sat in released OpenSSL versions from March 2012 until the fix on 7 April 2014.

Review the flows, not the lines. For every value from outside, follow it to each sink and check the control at each trust boundary. Then ask the questions a tool cannot: should this exist, and who may use it?

blocks.question: A pull request adds a new admin-only endpoint. In a diff-based review, what is the first thing to check?
options: That the endpoint actually enforces admin-only access on the server side
That the variable names follow the style guide
That the code has comments
That it has the best possible performance
blocks.explain: A new entry point is new attack surface. The cheat sheet's diff-based steps start with the impact on existing security controls and new attack vectors; a missing authorization check is invisible to most scanners.

blocks.question: What does the Heartbleed story suggest about a programme's choice of verification methods?
options: Static analysis tools catch every memory bug, so manual review is unnecessary
Manual review alone is enough
Different methods catch different bugs: a human audit and a fuzzing tool found it while common static analysers would not have, so programmes layer them
Bugs in widely used software are always found quickly
blocks.explain: Two methods found Heartbleed (Mehta's code review and Codenomicon's testing tool), while Wheeler reports several static analysers would have missed it. The bug also sat in releases for about two years. No single method is enough.

lessons.title: Reviewing a real-looking diff: three bugs and their fixes

blocks.md:
Time to review a pull request. Its title: "Add invoice search, invoice detail and supplier note". The app stores invoices; each belongs to one user (`owner_id`). The *supplier note* is free text written by the company that issued the invoice, so it comes from a different party than the reader. In this small test app the logged-in user's id comes from a header; treat `load_user` as a stand-in for the real login system, not as part of the review.

Step through the code below with the checklist from lesson 5. Each scene stops at one of the three new endpoints.

blocks.title: Pull request #412: three endpoints, three findings

scenes.caption: Setup: a SQLite database, and a before_request hook that sets g.user_id for every request. In production this would come from the session after login.
Search. The source is the q parameter (line 14). Line 17 builds SQL with an f-string, so q becomes part of the SQL code. ASVS v5.0.0-1.2.4 fails. Finding 1: SQL injection.
scenes.output: Tested on a copy: returned 2 rows, including user 2's invoice. The -- comments out the rest, and OR 1=1 is true for every row.

scenes.caption: Invoice detail. The query is parameterised, so no injection. But it selects by id only: any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the number. ASVS 8.2.2 fails. Finding 2: IDOR.
scenes.output: GET /invoices/2 as user 1: 200 OK with user 2's invoice.

scenes.caption: Supplier note. Ownership is checked (line 29), good. But line 33 glues text written by the supplier into HTML with no encoding. ASVS 1.2.1 fails. Finding 3: stored XSS.

blocks.prompt: Before reading on: the company runs Semgrep with a taint rule for request data reaching SQL, and GitHub's CodeQL default code scanning queries, on every pull request. Which of the three findings would the scanners report?
blocks.reveal:
**Only finding 1.** We ran both on this exact file. The Semgrep rule from lesson 8 reported lines 16 and 17 (the f-string passed to `execute` on line 15), and CodeQL's default suite reported one result, "SQL query built from user-controlled sources", on the same lines.

Finding 2 is a **missing** check: no dangerous data flow exists, the query is perfectly safe as SQL, it just returns the wrong row. Finding 3's source is a database row, which default rules do not treat as attacker-controlled. Two of three bugs needed the human reviewer.

blocks.caption: The fixed endpoints, tested on the same copy: the injection string now matches nothing (0 rows), user 1 gets 404 for user 2's invoice, and the note is returned as <script>... text. markupsafe.escape is the escaping function Flask's templates use.

blocks.md:
Why each fix works:

1. **Search**: the SQL text is now fixed and `q` travels separately as a bound parameter, so the database treats it only as a value to compare with `LIKE`. Code and data are on separate channels, as in *Injection attacks*.
2. **Detail**: the query adds `AND owner_id = ?`, so the ownership check happens in the same statement that fetches the row. Returning 404 for "exists but not yours" avoids confirming which ids exist.
3. **Note**: `escape()` converts `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes into HTML entities, so the browser displays the text instead of parsing it as markup. In a real app the better fix is to render through a template, where autoescaping applies to every variable by default.

Write the review comment the way you would want to receive it: the line, the attack in one sentence, the fix, and the ASVS ID or test to add.

**Defender view.** Prevent: the three requirements become tests (lesson 3) so the bugs cannot come back. Detect in production: database syntax errors and unusual `LIKE` patterns in application logs for injection probing; many 404s or 200s across sequential invoice ids from one account for IDOR enumeration, as in *Access control*; Content Security Policy violation reports for injected scripts. Respond: if the code shipped, search access logs for each pattern and treat reads of other users' invoices as a data breach to assess.

blocks.question: Which fix for finding 2 is correct?
options: Hide the invoice id in the URL by encoding it in base64
Use random UUIDs instead of integers, without any ownership check
Check ownership on the server: fetch with WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ? and return 404 otherwise
Hide the link to other users' invoices in the UI
blocks.explain: Encoding, random ids and hidden links only make ids harder to guess or see; none checks authorization. The ownership condition in the query enforces it on every request, which is what ASVS 8.2.2 asks.

blocks.question: Why did neither scanner flag finding 3, the stored XSS?
options: XSS cannot be detected by any tool
The note endpoint has an ownership check, which scanners treat as a sanitiser
f-strings are invisible to static analysis
The source is a database row written earlier by another party, and default rules do not treat database reads as untrusted input
blocks.explain: Taint rules start from configured sources, usually request data. Stored XSS takes a detour through the database, which breaks the chain unless a rule marks those reads as sources. Reviewers must ask who wrote the data.

lessons.title: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink

blocks.md:
**SAST** (static application security testing) means analysing source code for vulnerabilities without running it; "static" because the program sits still. The simplest SAST tools match text patterns, like searching for `execute(` and a `+` on the same line. They are fast and noisy. The useful ones do **taint analysis**.

The idea is familiar from Perl's *taint mode* ([perlsec](https://perldoc.perl.org/perlsec)): Perl marks data from outside the program (command-line arguments, environment variables, file input) as "tainted" and refuses to use it in commands that start a shell or modify files until it has been checked. Taint analysis applies the same idea to source code, without running it.

Four ingredients:

- **Source**: where untrusted data enters, such as `request.args.get(...)`.
- **Propagation**: operations that carry taint along. Concatenating a tainted string, formatting it into an f-string, or assigning it to another variable gives a tainted result.
- **Sanitiser**: an operation that removes the taint because its output is safe for the sink. `int(x)` cannot produce SQL syntax, so its result is clean.
- **Sink**: an operation where tainted data causes harm, such as the SQL string argument of `execute(...)`.

The tool reports a finding when a path exists from a source to a sink that passes through no sanitiser. Watch it work on four small endpoints.

blocks.title: Taint analysis walking four endpoints

scenes.caption: Endpoint 1. request.args.get is a source: q is tainted.
String concatenation propagates taint: sql is built from q, so sql is tainted too.
sql reaches the first argument of execute, a sink. Source to sink, no sanitiser on the way: report line 11. A true positive.
Endpoint 2. The source is wrapped in int(), a sanitiser in our rule: an integer cannot carry SQL syntax. item_id is clean, so the f-string on line 16 is not reported.
Endpoint 3. col is tainted. A human sees the allowlist check: col can only be 'title' or 'price' after line 22.
The tool does not understand that the if statement limits col's values, so col stays tainted and line 23 is reported. Safe code, reported anyway: a false positive.
Endpoint 4. q is tainted, but the SQL string is a constant and q is passed as a separate parameter, which is not the sink argument. Nothing to report.

blocks.md: This is the result we got by running a real rule (next lesson) on this file: findings at lines 11 and 23, nothing at 16 and 29. Real tools add much more: they know thousands of library sources and sinks, follow data across functions and files (**interprocedural** analysis), and track taint through objects and containers. Precision costs time: following every path across a large codebase is expensive, which is one reason tools disagree.

"No findings" does not mean "no bugs". Semgrep's own README warns that its free Community Edition analyses taint only within a single function or file, so it misses many true positives in security work. A flow that hops across files, or a source the rules do not know about, is invisible.

Source, propagation, sanitiser, sink. A finding is a path from a source to a sink with no sanitiser on it. False positives come from checks the tool cannot understand; false negatives come from sources, sinks or paths it does not model.

blocks.question: A developer writes `name = request.args.get('name').strip()` and then `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = '" + name + "'")`. What will a taint tool report, and is it right?
options: Nothing: strip() is a sanitiser
A false positive, because names are harmless
A finding: strip() only removes whitespace, so taint propagates to the sink, and the report is a true positive
Nothing: cursor.execute is not a sink
blocks.explain: strip() returns a modified copy of tainted text, so the result is still tainted. Only operations whose output cannot carry the attack, such as int() for SQL or encoding for HTML, are sanitisers.

blocks.question: Why did the tool report line 23 even though the code is safe?
options: Because the allowlist check limits values through a branch, and the tool's taint model does not treat that comparison as a sanitiser
Because ORDER BY is always dangerous
Because col was never assigned
Because abort(400) is a sink
blocks.explain: Taint tools reason about flows, not about which values survive a condition. Lesson 9 covers what to do about such false positives.

lessons.title: Writing rules: Semgrep and CodeQL on the same code

blocks.md: Two widely used tools let you write your own SAST rules. **Semgrep** is, in its README's words, a fast, open-source static analysis tool and "semantic grep for code": grep is the classic Unix text search, and *semantic* means Semgrep matches the code's structure rather than its characters, so its rules look like the code they find. **CodeQL** is GitHub's language and toolchain for code analysis. It first extracts your code into a database, then runs queries written in QL, a logic query language, against it. GitHub designed it for **variant analysis**: taking one known bug and searching for all its siblings.

A Semgrep taint rule is YAML with the four ingredients from lesson 7. `pattern-sources` lists where taint starts; `pattern-sanitizers` lists what cleans it; `pattern-sinks` says where it must not arrive. In the sink below, `pattern-inside` matches any call `$DB.execute($SQL, ...)`, where `$DB` and `$SQL` are **metavariables** (placeholders that match any expression), and `focus-metavariable: $SQL` narrows the sink to the first argument only. That one line is why the parameterised query in endpoint 4 is not reported: its tainted value is the second argument.

blocks.code:
rules:
  - id: flask-request-to-sql
    mode: taint
    languages: [python]
    severity: ERROR
    message: Request data reaches a SQL string. Use a ? placeholder and pass the value separately.
    pattern-sources:
      - pattern: flask.request.args.get(...)
      - pattern: flask.request.form.get(...)
    pattern-sanitizers:
      - pattern: int(...)
    pattern-sinks:
      - patterns:
          - pattern-inside: $DB.execute($SQL, ...)
          - focus-metavariable: $SQL

# run it (Semgrep Community Edition, installed with pip)
$ semgrep --metrics=off --config sqli-taint.yaml app.py
    app.py
   flask-request-to-sql
      Request data reaches a SQL string. Use a ? placeholder and pass the value separately.
       11| return {"rows": db.execute(sql).fetchall()}
       23| return {"rows": db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY {col}").fetchall()}
blocks.caption: The rule and its real output on lesson 7's app.py (output trimmed of banners). Line 11 is the true positive, line 23 the allowlisted false positive; the int() line and the parameterised line are correctly silent.

blocks.md: The CodeQL version uses library classes instead of hand-written patterns. `RemoteFlowSource` already knows Flask's `request` object and many other frameworks; `SqlExecution` knows sqlite3, many database drivers and ORMs, and `getSql()` picks the argument that holds the SQL text. `TaintTracking::Global` follows data across functions and files. The query below follows the structure in GitHub's documentation for Python data flow.

blocks.caption: The query, following the structure GitHub documents for Python data flow. @kind path-problem asks CodeQL to report the whole path from source to sink, not just the sink.

blocks.code:
$ codeql database create db --language=python --source-root=src
$ codeql database analyze db RequestToSql.ql --format=csv --output=out.csv
$ cut -d, -f5,6 out.csv
"/app.py","11"
"/app.py","23"
blocks.caption: We ran this with CodeQL CLI 2.27.4 on the same app.py: two results, lines 11 and 23, matching Semgrep. GitHub's standard py/sql-injection query, run on the same database, flagged the same two lines.

blocks.title: Four endpoints, ground truth against two tools

scenes.caption: Ground truth, decided by a human: only the search endpoint is exploitable. The int(), allowlist and parameter versions are safe.
Semgrep: flags search (true positive) and sorted (false positive), silent on item and safe (true negatives).
CodeQL, custom query and GitHub's standard one: exactly the same verdicts on this file. Both lose on the allowlist; neither misses the real bug here.
Lesson 6 showed the other side: on the invoice app, the same tools caught 1 of 3 real bugs. High agreement on simple injection says little about recall on logic bugs.

blocks.md: Licensing differs. Semgrep Community Edition is open source (LGPL-2.1). The CodeQL CLI's terms allow free use on open-source codebases, academic research and demonstrations; analysing private code needs a GitHub licence. Check before you wire either into a company pipeline.

Write a custom rule when a bug teaches you a pattern: after every incident or review finding, ask "where else does this pattern appear?" and encode it. That is variant analysis, and it turns one fix into a class fix.

blocks.question: In the Semgrep rule, what does `focus-metavariable: $SQL` achieve?
options: It speeds up the scan by skipping other files
It converts the rule from Python to SQL
It marks $SQL as a sanitiser
It makes only the first argument of execute() a sink, so tainted values passed as separate bound parameters are not reported
blocks.explain: Without it, the whole call would be the sink and endpoint 4, which passes q as a bound parameter, would be a false positive. Precise sinks are the main lever for reducing noise.

blocks.question: A Project Zero style team fixes a use-after-free and wants to find similar bugs across the codebase. Which use of CodeQL is this?
options: Fuzzing
Dependency scanning
Variant analysis: using a known bug as a seed to find similar problems
Secrets scanning
blocks.explain: CodeQL's documentation describes variant analysis as using a known vulnerability as a seed to find similar ones, and calls querying code with CodeQL the most efficient way to do it.

lessons.title: SAST in CI: false positives, triage and developer trust

blocks.md: Every scanner result falls in one of four boxes. A **true positive** (TP) is a real bug reported. A **false positive** (FP) is safe code reported as a bug. A **false negative** (FN) is a real bug not reported. A **true negative** (TN) is safe code left alone. Two ratios summarise a rule:

blocks.caption: Precision: of the alerts, how many were real. Recall: of the real bugs, how many were alerted.

blocks.title: Our two runs, counted

scenes.caption: app.py from lesson 7: 1 TP (search), 1 FP (allowlisted sort), 0 FN, 2 TN. Precision 1/2 = 50%, recall 1/1 = 100%.
The invoice app from lesson 6, counting its three real bugs: 1 TP (SQL injection), 0 FP, 2 FN (IDOR, stored XSS). Precision 100%, recall 1/3 = 33%. Same tools, very different picture.

blocks.md:
Both numbers matter, but precision decides whether developers keep listening. A rule that is wrong half the time trains people to click "ignore" on everything, including the true positives. Programmes that keep SAST alive in CI (continuous integration: the service that builds and tests every change automatically) follow a few habits:

- **Report only new findings** on a pull request. Old ones go to a backlog with an owner. Semgrep's `--baseline-commit` option shows only results not already present in a given commit.
- **Block only on high-confidence rules.** Noisier rules post comments but do not fail the build.
- **Suppress with a reason.** An inline suppression is fine when it says why and someone reviewed it; count suppressions per rule.
- **Measure each rule's false positive rate** from triage decisions and fix or retire the noisy ones.

blocks.code:
# CI step: fail the build only on findings this pull request introduces
semgrep scan --config rules/ --baseline-commit "$BASE_SHA" --error

# Triage of the allowlist false positive: a reviewed, explained suppression
    col = request.args.get("sort", "title")
    if col not in ("title", "price"):
        return {"error": "bad sort"}, 400
    # allowlisted above; reviewed by appsec 2026-11
    return {"rows": db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY {col}").fetchall()}  # nosemgrep: flask-request-to-sql
blocks.caption: --error makes Semgrep exit 1 when it finds something, which fails the CI job. The nosemgrep comment silences one rule on one line. We also tried rewriting the check as a dictionary lookup; the rule still fired, because taint flows through .get(), so a reviewed suppression was the honest fix.

blocks.prompt: A team turns on 400 SAST rules at once, blocking merges on every finding. In the first week the scanner reports 2,300 findings across the old codebase. What happens next, and what should they have done?
blocks.reveal:
Usually: builds go red everywhere, teams ask for an exemption, someone disables the check, and the tool loses credibility for years.

Better rollout: start with a handful of high-precision rules for the bug classes that hurt you most (injection, secrets), report only findings that a pull request **introduces**, send the existing 2,300 to a triaged backlog with owners, and add rules one at a time while watching each one's false positive rate. Trust is the scarce resource; spend it on true positives.

blocks.md: A suppression is a risk acceptance. If anyone can add `nosemgrep` without review, the cheapest way to pass CI is to silence the tool. Route suppressions in sensitive paths through CODEOWNERS (lesson 1) so AppSec sees them.

blocks.question: A rule fired 40 times last month. Triage marked 10 as real bugs and 30 as safe. What is its precision, and what should you do?
options: 25%, make it non-blocking and fix or retire it
75%, keep it as a blocking rule
40%, because it fired 40 times
Precision cannot be computed without false negatives
blocks.explain: Precision = 10 / (10 + 30) = 25%. Three of four alerts waste a developer's time. Keep it as a comment-only rule while you narrow its sinks or add sanitisers, or retire it.

blocks.question: Why report only findings introduced by a pull request?
options: Old findings are always false positives
Scanners cannot see old code
It makes recall 100%
It keeps the author responsible only for their own change, so the signal is actionable, while old findings are handled through a backlog with owners
blocks.explain: A developer can fix what they just wrote in minutes. Being blocked by someone else's five-year-old finding teaches them to bypass the tool.

lessons.title: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI

blocks.md: Static analysis reads code. Some bugs only show up when the program runs: a misconfigured server header, a login page that leaks whether a username exists, a parser that crashes on a strange input. Each testing method looks at the application from a different place, and a programme picks a combination. Tiny example: a missing security header is invisible in your Python code (the web server adds headers), obvious to a tool that sends a request and reads the response.

- **DAST** (dynamic application security testing) tests the running application from outside, like an attacker with a browser: it crawls pages and sends requests, then analyses responses. OWASP's DevSecOps Guideline calls it black-box testing because it needs no source code. The open-source example is **ZAP** (Zed Attack Proxy), a scanner that sits between a browser and the app.
- **IAST** (interactive application security testing) puts sensors, libraries loaded inside the application, that watch data flow and configuration while tests or people use the app, and report a vulnerability when tainted data actually reaches a sink at runtime. It sees inside like SAST and observes real execution like DAST, but only covers code that the tests exercise.
- **SCA** (software composition analysis), recalled from *Software supply chain security*: compares your dependency list or SBOM against vulnerability databases such as OSV.
- **Fuzzing**: feeding a program large numbers of generated, malformed inputs and watching for crashes, hangs or memory errors.

blocks.title: Where each method looks

scenes.caption: The parts of one web service: its source code, its dependencies, and the running process that real requests reach.
SAST reads the source code; SCA reads the dependency list or SBOM. Both work before anything runs, so they fit in every pull request.
DAST talks to the running app from outside, exactly like a user. It finds configuration and response problems but cannot point at the line of code.
IAST sits inside the running process. When a test request makes tainted data hit a sink, it reports the exact path, but only for code the tests reach.
A fuzzer drives one function, such as a parser, with millions of generated inputs and watches for crashes. Best for code that parses untrusted bytes.

blocks.code:
# DAST in CI: ZAP's baseline scan against a staging deployment
docker run -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable zap-baseline.py \
    -t https://staging.example.com
blocks.caption: Per ZAP's documentation, the baseline scan spiders the target for one minute by default, waits for passive scanning, and reports alerts as warnings. It does not perform attacks, which is why it is considered safe for CI. Run active scans only against systems you own or are authorised to test.

blocks.md:
**Fuzzing in CI.** Google's **OSS-Fuzz** runs continuous fuzzing for open-source projects; Google says it found thousands of security vulnerabilities and stability bugs by fuzzing Chrome components this way. For your own repositories, **ClusterFuzzLite** runs as part of CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Google Cloud Build, Prow): it fuzzes each pull request briefly to catch bugs before they land, runs longer batch fuzzing in the background, and supports C, C++, Java, Go, Python, Rust and Swift.

Heartbleed again: Codenomicon found it while building a new feature, SafeGuard, for Defensics, its protocol testing tool. Wheeler's analysis argues that **negative testing** (tests that send invalid input and check it is rejected) or fuzzing with memory checking would have caught it, while "mostly positive" test suites that only check correct inputs did not.

No method sees everything. SAST and SCA see code and dependencies early; DAST sees the deployed surface; IAST sees runtime paths the tests exercise; fuzzing sees parsers under abuse. Pick by what your application does: an API with a heavy parser needs fuzzing more than a static brochure site does.

blocks.question: A scanner reports that the production login page sends no Strict-Transport-Security header. Which method most naturally finds this?
options: SAST, by reading the Python code
SCA, by reading the lockfile
DAST, because the header is visible in the running app's HTTP responses
Fuzzing the password hashing function
blocks.explain: Headers are often added by the web server or proxy, not the application code, so only a tool that inspects real responses sees what users get.

blocks.question: Why can IAST miss a vulnerability that SAST finds?
options: IAST only reports on code paths that tests or users actually executed during the run
IAST cannot run in CI
IAST only works on compiled languages
IAST ignores SQL
blocks.explain: IAST observes real execution, which makes its findings precise, but untested code is never observed. SAST reasons about all paths, including ones nobody executed, at the price of false positives.

blocks.md:
A **secret** is anything that grants access by being known: passwords, API keys, cloud access keys, tokens, private keys, database connection strings. Tiny example: a developer tests an upload script with their cloud key pasted in, commits, and pushes. Deleting the line in the next commit does not help: git keeps every version, so the key sits in the repository's history for anyone with read access, and for everyone if the repository is public.

ASVS v5.0.0-13.3.1 (L2) says secrets must not be in source code or build artifacts and belong in a secrets management solution such as a key vault. Microsoft's SDL runs a credential and secret scanner in its pipeline. A programme stops secrets at three points: on the developer's machine, at push, and by scanning what already leaked.

**Git hooks** are scripts git runs at fixed points in its workflow; a **pre-commit hook** runs just before a commit is recorded and can refuse it. The **pre-commit** framework manages these hooks from a YAML file in the repository. **Gitleaks** is an open-source tool that detects secrets like passwords, API keys and tokens in git repositories and files, using rules made of regular expressions and entropy (a measure of randomness: real keys look random, ordinary words do not). Its README now says it is feature complete and will receive security patches only, so check the project's status when you adopt it; the hook pattern is the same for any scanner.

blocks.code:
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.24.2
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

# one-time setup per clone
$ pip install pre-commit
$ pre-commit install

# a commit with a hard-coded (made-up) AWS key
$ git commit -m "add upload"
Detect hardcoded secrets.................................................Failed
- hook id: gitleaks
- exit code: 1
Finding:     ... aws_access_key_id="REDACTED", aws_secret_access...
RuleID:      aws-access-token
File:        upload.py
Line:        2
WRN leaks found: 2
blocks.caption: The configuration from the Gitleaks README and the real (trimmed) output when we committed a file with an invented AWS key pair. The commit was refused; the second finding was a generic-api-key match on the secret key.

blocks.title: Three nets for one leaked key

scenes.caption: First net: the pre-commit hook on the laptop. Gitleaks finds the key and the commit is refused before it exists.
Hooks are local and optional: a clone without pre-commit installed, or SKIP=gitleaks, gets past. So the server checks too.
Second net: GitHub's push protection scans the push and blocks it with an explanation; the developer must remove the secret and push again.
Third net: if a secret ever lands (old history, a bypass), the response is to revoke it at the provider and issue a new one. Removing it from git is cleanup, not the fix.

blocks.md: Rewriting git history to remove a secret does not un-leak it. Forks, clones, CI caches and anyone who fetched in the meantime still have it. Treat any committed secret as compromised: rotate it, then look at the provider's logs for its use.

Defender view: detect leaked keys being used by alerting on API calls from unfamiliar networks for that key in your cloud audit logs. Prevent the whole class by giving CI short-lived credentials (OIDC, recalled from the supply chain course) and keeping long-lived keys in a vault, not in files.

blocks.question: A developer committed an API key, noticed, and pushed a second commit deleting it within a minute. What is the correct response?
options: None: the key is gone from the latest version
Make the repository private
Revoke the key at the provider, issue a new one, and check the key's usage logs
Squash the two commits
blocks.explain: The key is still in the first commit, and pushed history may already be cloned. Only revoking it removes its power. Then look for use between push and revocation.

blocks.question: Why does a programme need push protection on the server when every developer has a pre-commit hook?
options: Hooks run only where installed and can be skipped, so a server-side check is the control that cannot be bypassed by a single developer
Pre-commit hooks are slower
GitHub cannot read commits
Push protection replaces secret rotation
blocks.explain: Client-side checks give the fastest feedback; server-side checks give enforcement. The same pattern as access control: never rely only on the client.

lessons.title: Security champions, bug bounties and disclosure programmes

blocks.md:
Two problems remain after the tools. Inside the company, a small AppSec team cannot be present in 30 product teams. Outside, people will find bugs you missed, and you want them to tell you rather than sell or publish them. Programmes answer the first with **security champions** and the second with **disclosure programmes** and **bug bounties**.

A **security champion** is a developer who stays in their product team but takes on extra security training and a few hours a week of security work: first reviewer for risky changes (lesson 4's "champion review"), triage of scanner findings for their team, and the person who carries AppSec's guidance into planning. The champion is a multiplier, not a replacement for the AppSec team.

The OWASP Security Champions Guide, an open, vendor-neutral guidebook, lists ten principles for running such a programme: be passionate about security; start with a clear vision for the programme; secure management support; nominate a dedicated captain; trust your champions; create a community; promote knowledge sharing; reward responsibility; invest in your champions; and anticipate personnel changes.

The last one is the programme lesson from Equifax again: a role that depends on one person's goodwill disappears when they change teams. Champions need time in their sprint plan, recognition in their performance review, and a named successor.

Outside the company, a **VDP** (vulnerability disclosure policy, or programme) tells people how to report a vulnerability, what testing is allowed, and what happens next. A **bug bounty** is a VDP that also pays rewards for valid reports, often run on a platform such as HackerOne or Bugcrowd that handles intake and payment.

**Safe harbour** (a protection from liability for people who follow stated rules) is the policy language that matters most to researchers. disclose.io, an open project that publishes model policies, describes it as language that lets people acting in good faith, as the recipient defines it, report security issues without fear of legal repercussions. You learned the legal line in *Security basics*: authorisation is what separates research from crime, and a published policy is how a company grants it.

The US government made this mandatory for its own agencies. CISA's Binding Operational Directive 20-01 (2 September 2020) requires each federal civilian agency to publish a VDP that includes, among other things: which systems are in scope and which test methods are allowed; a statement that reports may be anonymous; a commitment not to recommend or pursue legal action against anyone whose research the agency concludes was a good faith effort to follow the policy, deeming that activity authorised; and a statement of when the reporter can expect acknowledgement.

CISA's Secure by Design pledge (lesson 19) asks software makers for the same: publish a VDP that authorises public testing, commits to no legal action for good-faith research, and allows public disclosure in line with coordinated disclosure practice. Recall security.txt (RFC 9116) from *Security basics*: it is how researchers find your contact and policy.

blocks.title: A report through a VDP, from finder to fix

scenes.caption: The researcher reads security.txt and the policy: scope, allowed tests, safe harbour. Reports go to the PSIRT (product security incident response team, the group that handles vulnerabilities in a company's products).
Report submitted, through a bounty platform or directly. The policy promised acknowledgement within a stated time.
The PSIRT validates it and hands it to the owning team with a deadline.
The team ships a fix. The PSIRT, often as a CNA (next lesson), assigns a CVE ID and publishes an advisory crediting the researcher.

blocks.code:
# Metrics BOD 20-01 asks agencies to report about their VDP (excerpt)
- number of reports received, and number found valid
- number of open valid reports, and their median age (days since receipt)
- number of open valid reports older than 90 days
- median time to validate a report
- median time to remediate or mitigate a valid report
- median time to first respond to the reporter
blocks.caption: From CISA's BOD 20-01. These are good metrics for any company's VDP, and lesson 18 uses the same idea, age of what is still open, for all vulnerabilities.

blocks.md: Champions scale security inside; a VDP with safe harbour invites help from outside. Both fail without the basics: someone answers the reports, and fixes have owners and deadlines.

blocks.question: A company launches a bug bounty without a safe-harbour clause, and its terms threaten legal action for "any unauthorised access". What is the likely effect?
options: More reports, because researchers like a challenge
Fewer good-faith reports, because researchers cannot be sure their testing counts as authorised
No effect: bounties are always legal
The company becomes a CNA
blocks.explain: disclose.io calls this a chilling effect: when the legal risk is unclear, good-faith researchers stay away. BOD 20-01 and the Secure by Design pledge both require a commitment not to pursue good-faith research.

blocks.question: Which practice makes a security champions programme survive a reorganisation?
options: Choosing only volunteers who love security
Anticipating personnel changes: budgeted time, recognition and a named successor for each champion
Making champions part of the AppSec team's headcount
Removing champions from their product teams
blocks.explain: This is one of the OWASP guide's ten principles. A role carried by goodwill alone disappears with the person.

lessons.title: CVE assignment and CNAs: who names a vulnerability

blocks.md:
Recall from *Security basics*: a CVE ID is the shared name of a publicly known vulnerability, and a **CNA** (CVE Numbering Authority) is an organisation authorised to assign IDs within its own scope. This lesson looks at the system from the side of a company that ships software, because a mature programme usually becomes a CNA for its own products.

Tiny example. Your company fixes a critical bug in its product. If you are a CNA, you reserve an ID, write the record (affected versions, weakness type, references) and publish it with your advisory, on your schedule. If you are not, someone else, possibly with less knowledge of your product, writes it for you.

The CVE Program is a hierarchy. The partner list behind cve.org (the data file in the CVE website's public repository, counted on 13 November 2026) has 567 organisations. Two are **Top-Level Roots**: MITRE, which also acts as the Secretariat running the program, and CISA. Eight are **Roots**, which recruit and manage CNAs in an area (for example Red Hat, and CISA's industrial control systems team). Three act as a **CNA-LR** (CNA of Last Resort), which assigns IDs when no other CNA's scope covers the product: MITRE, Red Hat and CISA ICS. The rest are CNAs: vendors (Apache, Microsoft), open-source projects (curl), bug bounty providers (HackerOne), and CERTs. One partner, CISA, is an **ADP** (Authorized Data Publisher) that adds enrichment to other CNAs' records.

blocks.title: The CVE Program hierarchy, and who wrote two real records

scenes.caption: Top: two Top-Level Roots, MITRE and CISA. Below them, Roots manage groups of CNAs.
Most IDs come from CNAs inside their own scope: a vendor for its products, a project for its code, a platform for reports it handles.
Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, was assigned by Apache as CNA for its own project, with its own advisory.

MOVEit, CVE-2023-34362, was assigned by MITRE acting as CNA of Last Resort. The CNA's record listed vendor, product, version and weakness as n/a; CISA's ADP container added CWE-89, product identifiers, KEV and SSVC data.

blocks.caption: Fetched from https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2023-34362. Machines matching this record against an inventory need the vendor, product and versions; the CNA container had them only inside the prose description.

blocks.md:
That record shows why the Secure by Design pledge has a CVE goal. It asks manufacturers to include accurate **CWE** (Common Weakness Enumeration: the bug type, here CWE-89, SQL injection) and **CPE** (Common Platform Enumeration: a standard product and version identifier) fields in every CVE record for their products, and to issue CVEs in a timely way for at least all critical or high-impact vulnerabilities that need customer action or are being exploited. CISA notes that a short-term rise in CVEs while a company removes a vulnerability class should count as success.

For your programme: becoming a CNA for your products means a documented process, a disclosure policy, and someone who writes good records. Publishing a CVE is not an admission of failure; it is how customers' scanners learn they must patch.

Fewer CVEs is not the same as fewer vulnerabilities. A vendor that fixes bugs silently looks clean while customers' scanners have nothing to match and never flag the old version. Judge vendors by how fast and how well they publish, not by the count.

blocks.question: A small open-source project with no CNA receives a valid report. Nobody else's scope covers it. Who can assign the CVE?
options: Only NIST
A CNA of Last Resort, such as MITRE
The researcher, by choosing any free number
Nobody: projects without a CNA cannot get CVEs
blocks.explain: CNA-LRs exist exactly for products outside every other CNA's scope. MITRE did this for MOVEit's CVE-2023-34362.

blocks.question: Why does the Secure by Design pledge ask for CPE fields in CVE records?
options: CPE encrypts the record
CPE gives a machine-readable product and version identifier, so scanners and inventories can match the CVE to affected installations automatically
CPE replaces the CVSS score
CPE names the researcher
blocks.explain: Without structured product and version data, matching a CVE to your inventory means a human reading prose. The MOVEit record's CNA container had n/a until CISA's ADP added CPEs.

lessons.title: Vulnerability management end to end: inventory, scans, deduplication

blocks.md:
Everything so far finds bugs in code you write. **Vulnerability management** handles the other flood: known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in everything you run, from your own services' dependencies to operating systems, databases and appliances bought from vendors. It is a pipeline: know what you have, find what is vulnerable, merge duplicates, decide what matters, give it to an owner with a deadline, confirm the fix.

Tiny example: on a Friday a critical CVE is announced in a logging library. The question "are we affected?" has an answer in minutes if step one, the inventory, exists, and in weeks if it does not.

blocks.title: The vulnerability management pipeline

scenes.caption: 1. Inventory: every asset (server, container image, application, appliance) with its owner and what software and versions it runs. Everything downstream depends on it.
2. Scan: network scanners, SCA on repositories, container image scanners and SBOM matching each report findings. Each sees part of the estate.
3. Normalise and deduplicate: three tools reporting the same CVE on the same host become one finding; findings that one upgrade fixes become one ticket.
4. Enrich and prioritise: add KEV status, EPSS, exposure and asset importance (lessons 15 and 16) to decide the order and the deadline.
5. Ticket to the owner named in the inventory, with an SLA (lesson 17). 6. Rescan to verify, then close. Unverified closes are how Equifax-style gaps hide.

blocks.md:
**Log4Shell** (CVE-2021-44228) is the case that tested every organisation's pipeline at once. Log4j is a Java logging library; a feature added in 2013, JNDI lookup support (JNDI, the Java Naming and Directory Interface, is Java's API for looking up objects in naming and directory services), let a logged string make the library fetch and run code from a remote server. A security engineer at Alibaba Cloud reported it to the Apache Software Foundation on 24 November 2021; it became public on 9 and 10 December, and CISA added it to KEV on 10 December.

The US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB), which reviews major incidents, found that no comprehensive "customer list" for Log4j existed, not even a list of where it was built into other software, and enterprises and vendors scrambled to discover where they used it. The organisations that responded best understood their use of Log4j and had mature processes to manage assets and assess risk; few could do it at the speed needed. One federal cabinet department reported spending 33,000 hours on its Log4j response.

Then came the churn. Within 18 days Apache published four CVEs and four upgrades, in the CVE records' dates: CVE-2021-44228 (10 Dec, fixed in 2.15.0), CVE-2021-45046 (14 Dec, the first fix was incomplete, fixed in 2.16.0), CVE-2021-45105 (18 Dec, denial of service through recursive lookups, fixed in 2.17.0) and CVE-2021-44832 (28 Dec, fixed in 2.17.1). The CSRB describes the resulting "patching fatigue", and its recommendation 6 is plain: develop the capacity to maintain an accurate IT asset and application inventory. It also judged Log4j an "endemic vulnerability" that will remain in systems for a decade or longer.

Deduplication matters most in exactly this storm. Apache's advisory notes that only the `log4j-core` JAR (Java archive, the file a Java library ships as) is affected; applications that ship only `log4j-api` are not. A pipeline that knows this closes many findings at once instead of opening tickets for them.

blocks.code:
from collections import defaultdict

# Raw findings from three tools (scanner, SCA, container scan)
raw = [
    {"tool": "netscan", "asset": "pay-api-1", "cve": "CVE-2021-44228", "pkg": "log4j-core 2.14.1"},
    {"tool": "sca",     "asset": "pay-api-1", "cve": "CVE-2021-44228", "pkg": "log4j-core 2.14.1"},
    {"tool": "sca",     "asset": "pay-api-1", "cve": "CVE-2021-45046", "pkg": "log4j-core 2.14.1"},
    {"tool": "image",   "asset": "pay-api-2", "cve": "CVE-2021-44228", "pkg": "log4j-core 2.14.1"},
    {"tool": "sca",     "asset": "search-1",  "cve": "CVE-2021-44228", "pkg": "log4j-api 2.14.1"},
]
OWNER = {"pay-api-1": "payments", "pay-api-2": "payments", "search-1": "search"}

def applies(f):                      # Apache: only log4j-core is affected
    return f["pkg"].startswith("log4j-core")

tickets = defaultdict(set)
for f in filter(applies, raw):
    # one ticket per owner and fix: upgrading the package closes every CVE in it
    tickets[(OWNER[f["asset"]], f["pkg"])].add((f["asset"], f["cve"]))

print(len(raw), "raw findings became", len(tickets), "ticket(s)")
for (owner, pkg), items in tickets.items():
    print(owner, pkg, sorted({a for a, _ in items}), sorted({c for _, c in items}))

# output
5 raw findings became 1 ticket(s)
payments log4j-core 2.14.1 ['pay-api-1', 'pay-api-2'] ['CVE-2021-44228', 'CVE-2021-45046']
blocks.caption: Real output. Five raw findings from three tools: the log4j-api one is dropped as not applicable, two tools reporting the same CVE on pay-api-1 merge, and both CVEs on both payments hosts fold into one ticket, because one upgrade fixes them all. Assets and owners are made up.

blocks.md: Group findings by the action that fixes them and by the owner who must act. Developers do not want 300 tickets for one library upgrade; they want one ticket listing the 300 places it fixes.

blocks.question: During Log4Shell, what separated the organisations that responded best, according to the CSRB?
options: They had the most expensive scanners
They understood where they used Log4j and had mature processes to manage assets, assess risk and mobilise people
They had no Java code
They waited for the final fix before acting
blocks.explain: The Board found exactly this, and noted few organisations could do it at the speed needed. The capability is built before the incident: the inventory and the owner list.

blocks.question: A scanner reports CVE-2021-44228 on a service whose only Log4j component is log4j-api 2.14.1. What should the pipeline do?
options: Open a critical ticket immediately
Mark it not applicable: Apache states only log4j-core is affected, and record the reason so the next scan does not reopen it
Delete the scanner
Upgrade Java
blocks.explain: Applicability checks cut noise. Recording the decision with its reason (Apache's advisory) keeps it from bouncing back on every scan; this is also what a VEX statement from the supply chain course expresses.

lessons.title: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs

blocks.md: Recall from *Security basics*: **CVSS** scores how severe a vulnerability is in general (0 to 10), **EPSS** estimates the probability it will be exploited in the next 30 days, and **KEV** is CISA's list of vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. That lesson ordered two bugs by hand. Here we do it at scale, on live data, and see how much each signal shrinks the queue.

blocks.title: How much each filter shrinks the queue (live data, 13 Nov 2026)

scenes.caption: All CVEs with an EPSS score on 13 November 2026: 406,184. Nobody can patch these in order.
CVEs with an NVD CVSS v3 severity of High or Critical: 77,461 + 30,847 = 108,308. Filtering by severity alone still leaves a six-figure list.
CVEs with EPSS of at least 0.1 (10% chance of exploitation activity in the next 30 days): 17,555.
CVEs in KEV: 1,781, every one with evidence of real exploitation. But 441 KEV entries have EPSS below 0.1, so an EPSS-only filter would skip a quarter of known-exploited bugs. Use both.

blocks.md:
Those are global counts; your queue is the subset that is actually installed somewhere you run. Take eight real CVEs as findings in an imagined company. Their NVD base scores range from 7.5 to 9.8, so sorting by CVSS alone would put an SSRF in an internal AI tool (CVE-2024-2057, LangChain, 9.8) level with MOVEit (9.8), and Heartbleed on an internet-facing VPN appliance (7.5) near the bottom.

The script below ranks them in three tiers: KEV first (exploited now), then EPSS of at least 0.1 (likely soon), then the rest, with internet-facing assets and higher CVSS first inside each tier. It downloads the KEV catalogue and queries FIRST's EPSS API live; if you run it later, scores will have moved.

blocks.code:
import json, urllib.request
KEV = "https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json"
EPSS = "https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve="

findings = [  # CVE, NVD CVSS v3.1 base, asset, internet-facing?
    ("CVE-2024-2057",  9.8, "internal LLM tool",   False),
    ("CVE-2023-38545", 9.8, "build agents (curl)", False),
    ("CVE-2023-34362", 9.8, "MOVEit server",       True),
    ("CVE-2024-27101", 9.1, "authz service",       False),
    ("CVE-2023-4863",  8.8, "laptop browsers",     False),
    ("CVE-2024-6387",  8.1, "SSH bastion",         True),
    ("CVE-2023-44487", 7.5, "HTTP/2 proxy",        True),
    ("CVE-2014-0160",  7.5, "old VPN appliance",   True),
]

def get(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "prio-demo"})
    return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30))

kev = {v["cveID"] for v in get(KEV)["vulnerabilities"]}
ids = ",".join(f[0] for f in findings)
epss = {d["cve"]: float(d["epss"]) for d in get(EPSS + ids)["data"]}

def tier(cve):
    if cve in kev: return 1                 # exploited now
    if epss.get(cve, 0) >= 0.1: return 2    # likely soon
    return 3                                # severity only

ranked = sorted(findings, key=lambda f: (tier(f[0]), not f[3], -f[1]))
for n, (cve, cvss, asset, exposed) in enumerate(ranked, 1):
    print(n, cve, "T%d" % tier(cve), "KEV" if cve in kev else "-",
          "epss=%.3f" % epss.get(cve, 0), cvss, asset)
blocks.caption: Our prioritiser. Asset names and exposure are made up; CVE IDs, CVSS (from NVD) and live KEV and EPSS data are real. It ran on 13 November 2026; its output is shown below the next figure.

blocks.title: The same eight findings, three ways (data of 13 Nov 2026)

scenes.caption: Sorted by NVD CVSS alone: three 9.8s tie at the top, and the internal LangChain SSRF ranks with MOVEit. Heartbleed and HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (a denial of service that resets many streams quickly), both being exploited, come last at 7.5.
EPSS as a percentage. Six of eight are above 78%; LangChain is 0.7% and SpiceDB 0.5%. Famous, old, widely scanned bugs score near 100%.

Final order, drawn as 9 minus rank so taller means sooner. KEV tier first, MOVEit on top because it is internet-facing and 9.8. OpenSSH and curl next on EPSS. LangChain and SpiceDB, high CVSS but low EPSS, go last.
